newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia PTT trade union pleased with Stet, OTE deal.
newsitem.headline: Serbia PTT trade union pleased with Stet, OTE deal.

text.p: The trade union of PTT Srbije on Friday rejected speculation the recent sale of 49 percent of its telecommunications company, Telekom Srbije, to Italian and Greek partners would mean lay-offs for thousands of people.

"The trade union was informed about the course of the negotiations, we had the right to make proposals and we are satisfied with the negotiations and the contract," PTT Srbije trade union president Srdjan Golubovic told reporters.

The telecom and postal units in the republic's monopoly PTT Srbije were recently separated under a special law, paving the way for setting up Telekom Srbija and sale of a 49-percent stake in it to foreign partners.

In Serbia's first major privatisation deal signed earlier this week, Italy's Stet acquired a 29 percent and Greece's OTE a 20 percent stake in Telekom Srbija, worth a total of 1.568 billion German marks.

Although the contract specifies there will be no lay-offs for a period of five years, fears rose among PTT Srbije's nearly 30,000 employees their jobs could be jeopardized once foreign capital stepped in.

"This is something new for us. Never in the past 70 years has anything that belongs to the 'society', such as public enterprise PTT Srbije, been sold to foreigners," Mihajlo Cirovic, editor of the trade union's paper, told Reuters.
He said the last time the state sold its wealth to foreigners was in the 1920s when stakes in the large Bor copper mines and Trepca lead and zinc mines were sold.

The country's socialist system provides job security and guaranteed minimum wages for most workers, maintaining high employment despite obvious workforce surpluses in a cash-strapped economy running at 40 percent of its capacity.

"The capitalist system is seen here as ruthless and people are afraid foreigners will just say they don't need quite so many workers, which is actually true," a PTT Srbije postal employee told Reuters.
But Golubovic said all Telekom Srbija decisions must be approved by a Board of Directors in which Serbia has a majority.
Some 16,500 workers in the less profitable postal unit feared they would be neglected, although the deal provides for investments in this part of PTT Srbije over the next eight years.
Funds from rent of premises as well as two percent of Telekom's gross profit would be invested in the postal system over the next eight years, Golubovic said.

Funds from licence fees collected from Telekom Srbija will be used to upgrade the postal system -- 135 million marks in the first year, 125 million in the second, and not less than 50 million marks in following years. -- Amra Kevic, Belgrade newsroom +381 11 222 4305
